st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The randomized study accepts the cluster’s task-specific, human-dependent account and materially extends it: AI substantially improves and partially equalises performance on a bounded analytical task, while residual differences depend on how users direct and integrate assistance. Its immediate AI-off follow-up also adds limited evidence of short-run carry-over, without claiming durable learning or organisational and labour-market effects.
qs: Overall, task duration is the only outcome for which we do not observe an equalizing pattern, and if anything, the estimates suggest modest divergence rather than convergence.18       Overall, these results establish the first main finding: AI substantially but incom- pletely narrows the education-based productivity gap while assistance is available.

The overall picture is one in which differences in outcomes among treated par- ticipants are not driven primarily by the intensity of assistant use, but by how the assistant is employed and how its outputs are integrated into participants’ own work.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The experiment supports the cluster’s account of substantial but bounded and uneven AI gains: assistance sharply narrows an education-based task-performance gap without eliminating the importance of underlying human capital. Its findings on engagement, residual unassisted differences, limited immediate carryover and weak organizational realism also reinforce the cluster’s emphasis on user capability, cautious extrapolation and workflow complements rather than autonomous substitution.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s conditional account. Its randomized experiment finds larger gains for lower-education participants on a fixed business task, while emphasizing that effects vary by task and setting, human capital still shapes effective use, and task-level gap compression does not establish broader wage or inequality effects.
qs: In the control group without AI, higher-education participants outperform lower-education participants by 0.548 standard deviations; with AI, this gap falls to 0.139 standard deviations, closing about three- quarters of the initial gap.

Taken together, the emerging evidence suggests that generative AI often raises performance and compresses the productivity distribution within relatively homo- geneous groups of workers, though heterogeneous effects can vary across settings and tasks.

kp.k: Experiment isolates education-based differences in AI-assisted business performance
kp.d: Cruces, Fernandez Meijide, Galiani, Gálvez and Lombardi report a preregistered online experiment conducted in Argentina between September and November 2025. The analysis includes 1,174 adults aged 25–45: 520 low-education and 654 high-education participants. Low education means a high school diploma with no postsecondary education or less than half a postsecondary degree; high education means more than half completed. Participants received randomized access to an embedded GPT-4.1 assistant and completed one of three self-contained business diagnosis and email-writing tasks. This is cross-domain evidence about general business work, not a study of legal services.
qs: We obtained a sample of 1,174 individuals, 520 low-education and 654 high-education.
The AI assistant is based on OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 model and, for the treatment group, is embedded in the experiment interface.
Importantly, our task is self-contained and does not rely on domain or firm-specific knowledge, allowing us to study AI’s effects on performance in a general business problem-solving setting.

kp.k: AI closes approximately three-quarters of the education performance gap
kp.d: AI access raises the overall task score by 1.242 standard deviations for low-education participants and 0.834 for high-education participants, standardized against the low-education control group. Both effects and the 0.408 SD difference between treatment effects are significant at the 1% level. The education gap falls from 0.548 SD without assigned AI access to 0.139 SD with access, closing approximately 75%. The remaining assisted gap is not statistically significant at conventional levels (p=0.110), so the point estimates indicate incomplete convergence without establishing a statistically significant residual difference.
qs: The overall score increases by 1.242 SD for those in the low-education group, whereas the impact of the assistant for high-education subjects is 0.834 SD (both estimates are statistically significant at the 1% level).
the treatment closes 75% of the performance gap between low- and high-education participants with no access to the AI assistant.
High vs. low education (treatment): ∆=0.139 (pv=0.110)

kp.k: Performance convergence extends beyond improved writing
kp.d: The overall score weights content two-thirds and writing one-third. Low-education participants experience larger treatment effects in writing by 0.382 SD and in content by 0.389 SD, both significant at the 1% level. Correct root-cause identification rises from 49.5% to 84.1% for low-education participants and from 64.7% to 88.1% for high-education participants; the differential treatment effect is 11.2 percentage points, significant at 5%. Dispersion among treated participants argues against the gap reduction being mechanically produced by universal convergence to perfect scores.
qs: The main performance measure is an overall score, calculated as a weighted average of the two components (two thirds content, one third writing).
The equalizing effect of AI assistance operates through improvements in both dimensions of performance in our task.

the dispersion in scores for treated participants indicates that the larger gains observed among low-education participants are not mechanically driven by a general convergence from a lower baseline toward a perfect score.

kp.k: Completion times improve without an equalizing pattern
kp.d: AI reduces low-education participants’ task duration by 0.961 minutes from a 10.697-minute control mean, significant at 10%, and high-education participants’ duration by 1.514 minutes from a 10.423-minute control mean, significant at 1%. The difference between these treatment effects is not statistically significant. Unlike task quality, completion time therefore does not exhibit the same education-gap compression; duration is measured in minutes and top-coded at 20.
qs: However, the difference in treatment effects across groups is not statistically significant.
Overall, task duration is the only outcome for which we do not observe an equalizing pattern, and if anything, the estimates suggest modest divergence rather than convergence.

kp.k: Immediate unassisted gains do not establish durable learning
kp.d: After the task, participants immediately answered an open-ended root-cause question and two multiple-choice questions without AI. Prior AI access improves the overall follow-up score by 0.171 SD for low-education participants, significant at 5%, and by a statistically insignificant 0.071 SD for high-education participants. The treated education gap remains 0.200 SD, significant at 5%; the difference between follow-up treatment effects is not significant (p=0.398). Improvements are concentrated in the open-ended response, with no significant multiple-choice effects. The authors interpret these results as inconsistent with gains being purely contemporaneous delegation, but explicitly distinguish short-run carry-over from lasting skill formation.
qs: The estimates therefore capture short-run unassisted performance after AI exposure, not durable skill formation.
their follow-up score rises by 0.171 SD (significant at the 5% level).
For high-education individuals, the estimated treatment effect is smaller (0.071 SD) and not statistically significant.

kp.k: Engagement predicts carry-over despite similar AI-assisted output quality
kp.d: An exploratory analysis divides the 562 treated participants by above- or below-median task time, used as an engagement proxy, and by the share of task components for which AI help was requested. High-assistance participants achieve similarly strong main-task scores with high or low engagement: 1.878 versus 1.972 SD (p=0.206). Their follow-up scores differ substantially: 0.732 versus 0.065 SD (p<0.01). These observational relationships support the authors’ interpretation that exposure to a good answer alone is insufficient for carry-over; they do not identify a randomized causal effect of engagement.
qs: The second captures participants’ own engagement with the task, which we proxy with whether the participant spent more or less time on the task than the treatment-group median.
Intensive AI assistance is therefore sufficient to generate strong submitted answers, even when participants spend relatively little time engaging with the task.
Follow-up performance is also high among participants with high engagement but low AI assistance.

kp.k: Education relates to interaction quality rather than use intensity
kp.d: Chat-log analysis covers 471 treated participants who used the assistant. Both education groups send almost three messages and request help on approximately 61% of task components. Higher-education participants provide more detailed reasoning instructions (0.174 SD), are 6.7 percentage points more likely to begin with a highly specific prompt, and 7.5 points more likely to use a structured workflow. Full copying of AI output occurs in 70.2% of low-education users’ responses versus 60.1% of high-education users’ responses. The authors present these patterns as associations that help explain substantial convergence alongside continuing differences in effective tool use, not causal effects of particular prompting strategies.
qs: Overall, there are no meaningful differences between the two groups in the intensity of their interaction with the assistant.

Most participants rely on AI-generated content in their final output: 64% of final submissions include a full copy-paste of AI-generated text, and 34% partially rely on AI-generated text; only a small minority rely exclusively on self-generated content.

Relatedly, the correlations between AI use patterns and task scores reported in Appendix Table A.6 should be interpreted as associations, not as causal effects of particular interaction strategies on performance.

kp.k: Estimates concern access amid incomplete adoption and suspected contamination
kp.d: Among treated participants, 84% use the assistant during the task: 81% of low-education and 86% of high-education participants. The authors classify an estimated 13% of controls as suspected external-AI users, using page exits, textual indicators and abrupt word-count increases; estimated rates are 11% and 15% by education group. Their main estimates are intent-to-treat effects of access, not effects of actual usage. Of 1,795 eligible randomized participants, 1,174 complete the experiment; completion rates are 64% in treatment and 66% in control (p=0.373), with no significant within-education treatment differences reported.
qs: Takeup was high, with 84% of treated participants using the virtual assistant during the task (81% low education and 86% high education).
Combining both sources of evidence yields an overall noncompliance rate of 13%.
Our focus,  however, is on the effect of access rather than usage per se.

kp.k: Alternative grading methods support the reported performance findings
kp.d: The main grades average ten GPT-5-mini scoring iterations using preregistered criteria and task-specific rubrics. Robustness checks use Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini Flash 3.0, and three independently developed AI grading procedures, including comparative Elo ratings. Two blinded human graders assess 117 responses; the average human score correlates with the main AI score at Pearson 0.951 and Spearman 0.957. The authors also report stability under added controls, exclusion of low-quality responses and alternative education definitions. The document remains a working paper rather than a peer-reviewed publication.
qs: we run the grading procedure ten times and use the average score across all iterations.
we find a Pearson correlation of 0.951 and a rank-correlation of 0.957 between the AI-generated grades and the average of the manually generated grades, with little variation across graders.
Across all checks, the estimated treatment effects and their difference across education groups remain stable and consistent with the main results.

kp.k: Task-level equalization does not imply reduced labour-market inequality
kp.d: The authors interpret AI as relaxing constraints in problem structuring, organization and written communication that bind more strongly for less-educated participants, rather than equalizing underlying abilities. They explicitly do not predict wage or aggregate inequality effects from this experiment. Translation into labour-market outcomes depends on adoption, effective use, engagement, organizational task allocation, policy and equilibrium adjustments. They caution that equalization could attenuate or reverse on tasks involving skills current AI cannot readily replicate, or as model capabilities change.
qs: Generative AI does not eliminate the role of human capital, nor does it equalize fundamental abilities.
Accordingly, we do not interpret our estimates as direct predictions about wage effects or aggregate equilibrium inequality.
The equalizing pattern documented here may attenuate or reverse on tasks that rely more heavily on interpersonal coordination or other skills that current AI cannot easily replicate.
As capabilities expand, the relative gains for the two groups could shift, potentially attenuating or reversing the pattern.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Cruces and co-authors find that AI access substantially narrows education-based differences in business problem-solving performance, with modest immediate carry-over after assistance is removed.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study, not a study of legal services. The authors report that access to a GPT-4.1 assistant raises overall task scores by 1.242 standard deviations for lower-education participants and 0.834 for higher-education participants, measured relative to the lower-education control group. The education gap falls from 0.548 to 0.139 SD, closing approximately 75%; the differential treatment effect is significant at 1%, while the remaining assisted-performance gap is not statistically significant (p=0.110). Improvements occur in both content and writing. Completion time falls by 0.961 minutes for lower-education participants and 1.514 minutes for higher-education participants, without a statistically significant difference between these effects. On the immediate unassisted follow-up, lower-education participants gain 0.171 SD (significant at 5%); the higher-education gain of 0.071 SD is not significant. A 0.200 SD education gap remains in treated participants' follow-up scores. The authors interpret these results as task-level equalization rather than equalization of underlying abilities. Their exploratory analyses associate better follow-up performance with sustained engagement and associate higher education with somewhat more effective prompting and integration of AI output.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main claims rest on a preregistered randomized online experiment; explanations involving engagement and interaction strategies rest on exploratory associations.
pts.d: The experiment randomized AI access among eligible adults in Argentina. The analysis includes 1,174 completers out of 1,795 eligible randomized participants, with 520 classified as lower education and 654 as higher education. Participants completed one of three self-contained business scenarios requiring diagnosis, a proposed solution, and an email response, followed immediately by unassisted questions. Main estimates are intent-to-treat effects of access, not effects of actual use: 84% of treated participants used the assistant, while the authors estimated suspected external AI use among 13% of controls. Completion rates were similar across arms. Overall task scores weight content two-thirds and writing one-third. GPT-5-mini applied preregistered scoring criteria over ten grading iterations; robustness checks used alternative models, independently developed grading procedures, controls, and education definitions. In a 117-response manual validation sample, AI scores correlated 0.951 with the average human grade. Chat-log analysis covers 471 treated users. The engagement analysis uses time spent as a proxy for engagement and requested assistance across task components as a proxy for assistance intensity; neither behavior was randomized. The document identifies itself as a working paper that has not been peer-reviewed.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern short-run performance under embedded access and basic onboarding, not durable learning or predicted wage and employment effects.
pts.d: Fieldwork took place between September and November 2025; the supplied paper is dated February 2026, revised May 2026. Participants used GPT-4.1 in an incentivized experiment averaging 21 minutes overall. Follow-up questions were administered immediately, despite their hypothetical narrative referring to a meeting one week later. The assistant was preloaded with the informational report, and treated participants received a tutorial. The task required no industry- or firm-specific knowledge. The authors explicitly distinguish immediate carry-over from durable skill formation and do not interpret their estimates as direct predictions about wages or aggregate inequality. They condition broader effects on adoption, access, engagement, organizational task allocation, policy, and equilibrium adjustments. They suggest equalization could weaken or reverse for tasks relying on interpersonal coordination or as model capabilities change.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Both education groups benefit on assisted tasks, but lower-education adults gain more; broader distributional consequences remain conditional.
pts.d: The studied population comprises Argentine adults aged 25–45 who could participate using a personal computer, rather than employees selected within a particular firm or profession. Lower education means a high-school diploma with no postsecondary study or less than half a postsecondary degree completed; higher education means more than half completed, including graduates of university and non-university tertiary programs. Both groups obtain substantial assistance, with larger task-quality gains for the lower-education group. Among assistant users, lower-education participants more frequently fully copy AI text, while higher-education participants more often partially incorporate it and show somewhat more structured interactions. The authors suggest AI can relax constraints in problem structuring, organization, and written communication, but warn that unequal adoption and effective use may preserve or widen inequality outside the experiment. No direct claims are established about lawyers, law firms, legal clients, or legal markets.
